title: Motion and relative velocity in three dimensions
objective: Differentiate vector trajectories and transform relative positions and velocities between stated inertial frames.
why: A camera on a moving platform and a stationary camera can record different paths for the same object. Neither description is useful unless its observer and coordinate axes are specified. Componentwise calculus lets you reconstruct the motion, and frame transformations explain which velocities change and why constant-velocity observers agree about acceleration.

prerequisites.label: Differential calculus preparation
prerequisites.note: This course's lesson pack is under construction. Review derivatives of polynomials and the chain rule through the linked free calculus resource if needed.

sections.heading: A trajectory assigns a vector to every modeled time
paragraphs: In fixed orthonormal Cartesian axes, write $\mathbf r(t)=x(t)\hat{\mathbf i}+y(t)\hat{\mathbf j}+z(t)\hat{\mathbf k}$. Each component is a signed position coordinate in meters. A vector trajectory is more than a geometric curve: it also specifies when the object occupies each point, so two objects can follow the same curve at different speeds.

Use one shared time parameter for all three components. Evaluating x at 2 s and y at 3 s generally constructs a point the object never occupied. A time-position table therefore groups all components at each event time. A projection onto the xy plane omits z and cannot establish a full three-dimensional length or speed.

The displacement between two events is $\Delta\mathbf r=\mathbf r(t_2)-\mathbf r(t_1)$, and average velocity is $\Delta\mathbf r/(t_2-t_1)$ for t₂>t₁. This secant direction need not equal the tangent direction at either endpoint. A return to the starting point gives zero average velocity even if the intermediate path is long.

Coordinate axes in this lesson keep their orientation. Rotating axes have time-dependent basis vectors, whose derivatives contribute additional terms. The simple component rules below must not be applied unchanged to a rotating turntable or rotating Earth coordinates when rotation effects matter.

sections.heading: Differentiate components before taking a magnitude
paragraphs: Instantaneous velocity is $\mathbf v=d\mathbf r/dt=(dx/dt,dy/dt,dz/dt)$ in fixed Cartesian axes. Acceleration is $\mathbf a=d\mathbf v/dt$. Apply the one-dimensional derivative rule separately to each coordinate, while retaining one common time and the coordinate labels.

For r(t)=(1+2t,-2+t²,3-t³) in SI shorthand, v(t)=(2,2t,-3t²) and a(t)=(0,2,-6t). At t=1 s the velocity is (2,2,-3) m/s. Its speed is $|\mathbf v|=\sqrt{2^2+2^2+(-3)^2}=\sqrt{17}$ m/s, not the sum 2+2-3 and not the derivative of |r|.

For nonzero velocity, its unit direction is v/|v| and is tangent to the trajectory. The acceleration can have a component along velocity, which changes speed, and a perpendicular component, which changes direction. Acceleration therefore need not point along either position or velocity. A constant speed does not guarantee zero acceleration.

The scalar rate of change of speed, when |v|≠0, is $d|\mathbf v|/dt=(\mathbf v\cdot\mathbf a)/|\mathbf v|$. This extends the one-dimensional sign rule. A positive dot product increases speed; a negative one decreases speed; a zero dot product means no instantaneous speed change, even when the acceleration vector is nonzero. At zero velocity, examine the local motion separately instead of dividing by zero.

sections.heading: Distance from the origin is a different quantity from traveled distance
paragraphs: The magnitude |r| is separation from a selected origin. For r≠0, differentiating $|\mathbf r|^2=\mathbf r\cdot\mathbf r$ gives $d|\mathbf r|/dt=(\mathbf r\cdot\mathbf v)/|\mathbf r|$. This is a signed radial rate. It can be negative when the object approaches the origin, zero for instantaneously perpendicular motion, or positive when separation grows.

Speed is |dr/dt|; radial rate is d|r|/dt. The order of magnitude and differentiation matters. At an event with r=(3,0,0) m and v=(0,4,0) m/s, speed is 4 m/s while the radial rate is zero. The object is moving, but its separation from the origin has zero first derivative at that instant.

Traveled distance over an interval is $d=\int_{t_1}^{t_2}|\mathbf v(t)|\,dt$. It is at least the straight-line endpoint separation |Δr|. Integrating each velocity component first and then taking the magnitude gives |Δr|, not generally the path length. A curved path loses information when replaced by its endpoint chord.

Unlike speed under a fixed-origin translation, radial rate depends on the chosen origin because its direction vector r changes. Its magnitude cannot exceed speed: a projection onto one radial direction cannot be longer than the full velocity vector. The radial formula is undefined at r=0; this does not make the velocity vector itself undefined.

sections.heading: Integrate vector acceleration with vector initial conditions
paragraphs: Reconstruction is also componentwise: $\mathbf v(t)=\mathbf v_0+\int_0^t\mathbf a(s)\,ds$ and $\mathbf r(t)=\mathbf r_0+\int_0^t\mathbf v(s)\,ds$. Each integral represents three scalar integrals. Supply all components of the initial velocity and position; a value for only one axis does not determine the others.

For constant vector acceleration, $\mathbf v=\mathbf v_0+\mathbf a t$ and $\mathbf r=\mathbf r_0+\mathbf v_0t+\mathbf a t^2/2$. These equations combine three one-dimensional calculations but still describe one object at one time. When acceleration varies, integrate its actual components instead.

Independent component bookkeeping does not imply that the physical causes are independent. A resistance force can depend on total speed, coupling all components through |v|. A circular path imposes geometric constraints between coordinates. You may solve each component separately only after accounting for such shared forces or constraints.

For ideal projectile motion without air resistance, the assumed acceleration is (0,-g,0), so horizontal velocity stays constant while vertical velocity changes. That separability follows from the force model; it is not a universal property of any object that travels through the air. The next lesson will state and test those projectile assumptions explicitly.

sections.heading: Name both the moving object and its observer
paragraphs: A velocity is always relative to a reference frame. Let v_RG mean the velocity of robot R relative to ground G, v_RP the robot relative to platform P, and v_PG the platform relative to ground. Using parallel nonrotating axes and a shared classical time, the observer chain is $\mathbf v_{RG}=\mathbf v_{RP}+\mathbf v_{PG}$.

To obtain the robot velocity seen from the platform, rearrange to v_RP=v_RG-v_PG. Subtract corresponding components, not speed magnitudes. If both robot and platform move east at 3 m/s relative to the ground, the robot is at rest relative to the platform. If the robot moves west at 3 m/s, the platform sees it moving west at 6 m/s.

Reversing the roles of object and observer changes the sign: v_PR=-v_RP. This differs from merely changing which direction you call positive, although both operations can reverse component signs. Write the subscripts in words before substituting numbers when a problem includes several moving objects.

For a planar current or conveyor problem, combine the full vectors. A robot with velocity (1,2,-1) m/s relative to a platform moving at (3,-1,0) m/s relative to the ground has ground velocity (4,1,-1) m/s. Its ground speed sqrt(18) is neither the sum nor generally the difference of the two given speeds.

These addition rules use the Galilean approximation: a common time and speeds small compared with light speed. Relativistic velocity transformations are outside this mechanics model. State this limit rather than treating classical vector addition as universally exact.

sections.heading: Track the moving origin at the same time
paragraphs: Suppose the moving frame's origin starts at ground position R₀ and travels with constant velocity U. Its ground position is $\mathbf R(t)=\mathbf R_0+\mathbf U t$. If the axes remain parallel and share their scale, the object's moving-frame position is $\mathbf r'(t)=\mathbf r(t)-\mathbf R_0-\mathbf U t$. In these frame transformations a prime labels a moving-frame quantity; it does not denote differentiation. We write time derivatives explicitly as d/dt.

This equation subtracts two positions at the same event time. Subtracting U directly from r would mix velocity and position units. Omitting R₀ would silently assume the two origins coincided at t=0. Both errors can produce a plausible-looking picture with an incorrect numerical offset.

Differentiate once to get $\mathbf v'=\mathbf v-\mathbf U$. Differentiate again to get $\mathbf a'=\mathbf a$ because U is constant. Thus these two inertial frames generally disagree about positions, velocities, and speeds but agree about acceleration. Changing only the initial origin offset affects positions without changing velocities.

An observer can momentarily match the object's velocity, making v'=0 at that instant, while a' remains nonzero. Matching one instantaneous velocity does not create a frame in which an accelerating object remains at rest for an interval. Maintaining that match would require an accelerating observer, outside the constant-U transformation.

sections.heading: Check when an observer is no longer inertial
paragraphs: For a translating, nonrotating origin with a general trajectory R(t), differentiating r'=r-R gives v'=v-dR/dt and $\mathbf a'=\mathbf a-d^2\mathbf R/dt^2$. If the observer acceleration A=d²R/dt² is nonzero, the two acceleration vectors differ by A.

Relative to a known inertial ground frame, nonzero translational acceleration makes the observer frame noninertial. Later, a force equation written there needs the appropriate inertial-force term. The kinematic subtraction a'=a-A remains valid for this nonrotating translation; what changes is whether the simplest inertial form of Newton's law can be used without extra terms.

Rotation requires additional terms even when the observer's origin stays fixed. We are not modeling rotation in this lesson's investigation. A fixed origin alone does not establish an inertial frame: both its translation and the time dependence of its axis directions matter.

Check a frame calculation by reconstructing the original: r'+R must equal r, and v'+U must equal v. Check that the time and axes match, that each subtraction combines equal units, and that every claimed acceleration invariance rests on constant observer velocity and no rotation. A correct magnitude does not excuse a wrong direction or observer convention.

examples.title: Differentiate a full trajectory and separate two rates
examples.prompt: For r(t)=(1+2t,-2+t²,3-t³) in meters with t in seconds, find position, velocity, acceleration, speed, and the radial rate at t=1 s.

steps.reason: Evaluate position but differentiate each coordinate before evaluating velocity.
A second componentwise derivative gives acceleration; fixed axes contribute no derivative terms.
Speed uses every velocity component and is nonnegative.
The negative radial rate says separation from the origin decreases at that instant, while the object still travels with positive speed.

examples.conclusion: Speed is sqrt(17) m/s and radial rate is -2/sqrt(14) m/s. Interchanging magnitude and differentiation would answer the wrong question.

examples.title: Integrate three acceleration components
examples.prompt: A particle has a(t)=(2,0,-4t) m/s² for t in seconds, v(0)=(0,-1,2) m/s, and r(0)=(1,2,3) m. Find r and v at 2 s.

steps.reason: Integrate each acceleration component and include the corresponding initial velocity. Zero y acceleration leaves y velocity at -1 m/s.
Integrate velocity and include each initial position.
Evaluate all three components at the same event time.
Differentiating the result checks the initial velocity and supplied acceleration. The position at zero also matches (1,2,3).

examples.conclusion: The changing z acceleration requires an integral. Inserting a_z(2)=-8 m/s² into a constant-acceleration position formula would incorrectly assign that value to the whole interval.

examples.title: Compose a robot's velocity through an observer chain
examples.prompt: A robot moves at v_RP=(1,2,-1) m/s relative to a platform. The platform moves at v_PG=(3,-1,0) m/s relative to the ground. Find v_RG and reverse the robot-platform relationship.

steps.reason: The frame chain R relative to P, then P relative to G, supplies R relative to G.
Combine vectors first, then compute the requested speed.
Reversing object and observer reverses the relative velocity.
Reconstruct the given robot-platform velocity as an independent direction check.

examples.conclusion: The ground velocity is (4,1,-1) m/s. Adding the scalar speed magnitudes would erase directions before they can combine.

examples.title: Include the initial offset of a moving origin
examples.prompt: At t=2 s the object's ground position is (8,1,4) m. A frame origin starts at R₀=(-2,1,3) m and moves at constant U=(3,-1,2) m/s with parallel axes. Find the object's position in that frame.

steps.reason: Move the observer origin to the same time as the object event.
Subtract positions componentwise. Velocity U only becomes a position change after multiplication by elapsed time.
Adding the origin position reconstructs the ground position.

examples.conclusion: The relative position is (4,2,-3) m. Subtracting only Ut would omit the nonzero initial origin offset.

examples.title: Momentary rest in a moving frame is not permanent rest
examples.prompt: At t=2 s an object's ground velocity is (3,5,-2) m/s and its acceleration is (0,2,0) m/s², constant near that time. Choose a nonrotating observer with constant U=(3,5,-2) m/s. Compare relative velocity at 2 s and 2.5 s.

steps.reason: The observer matches the object's velocity at this one instant.
Observer velocity is constant, so its acceleration is zero. The object's acceleration persists.
Accumulating the nonzero acceleration over the next half second produces a nonzero relative velocity.

examples.conclusion: The object is at rest relative to this observer only momentarily. An observer that keeps matching it would have to accelerate and would not be the same constant-velocity inertial frame.

guided.title: Subtract the observer, then interpret the result
guided.setup: In the ground frame, an object has velocity (5,-2,1) m/s and acceleration (0,2,-1) m/s². A nonrotating observer translates at constant U=(2,1,-1) m/s. Use the same axis directions and time.
before: The object's relative velocity is its ground velocity minus U, component by component.
The relative speed is the nonnegative norm of that relative velocity vector.
To transform acceleration, differentiate U. A constant velocity contributes zero acceleration.

question.prompt: Find all three relative velocity components and the relative speed. Decide what happens to acceleration.

fields.label: Relative speed
fields.help: Use sqrt(...) and keep the value exact.

options.label: It remains (0,2,-1) m/s² because the observer velocity is constant
options.feedback: Differentiating v'=v-U removes the constant U, so acceleration is unchanged.

options.label: It becomes (-2,1,0) by subtracting the observer velocity
options.feedback: That subtraction mixes acceleration and velocity units. Differentiate the velocity transformation instead.

options.label: It must be zero because the observer moves at constant velocity
options.feedback: The observer acceleration is zero; the object's acceleration need not be. They are different bodies.

hints: The relative velocity is (3,-3,2) m/s, so its squared speed is 9+9+4.
Speed is sqrt(22) m/s. The same acceleration (0,2,-1) m/s² is measured in both nonrotating inertial frames.
explanation: The relative velocity is (3,-3,2) m/s and its magnitude is sqrt(22) m/s.
Adding U back recovers (5,-2,1) m/s. Because dU/dt=0, the acceleration remains (0,2,-1) m/s².
question.answerSummary: Relative velocity (3,-3,2) m/s; speed sqrt(22) m/s; acceleration unchanged.

guided.after: State whose velocity is relative to whom. Swapping object and observer would reverse all three relative velocity components while retaining their magnitude.

interaction.prompt: Predict velocity seen from the moving observer and compare accelerations. Reveal the same trajectory in two coordinate systems. Change the observer's initial origin, then its velocity, and explain which quantities change.

summary: Differentiate or integrate each component in fixed Cartesian axes, using the same time and complete vector initial conditions.
Speed is |dr/dt|. The derivative of |r| is a signed radial rate with a different physical meaning.
Travel distance integrates speed. The magnitude of integrated velocity gives only endpoint separation.
Name the object and its observer: v_RG=v_RP+v_PG. Combine components before magnitudes.
For a translating origin R₀+Ut, r'=r-R₀-Ut and v'=v-U. Units and time must match.
Constant observer velocity and nonrotating axes preserve acceleration. An accelerating observer requires subtracting its acceleration; rotating frames need additional terms.
Classical frame transformations assume a shared time and speeds small compared with light speed.
retrieval: At t=2 s, differentiate r(t)=(t²,3t,1-t) m and find speed. Then find velocity relative to an observer moving at U=(1,0,-1) m/s. Explain whether the acceleration changes. To check after working: ground velocity (4,3,-1) m/s, speed sqrt(26) m/s, relative velocity (3,3,0) m/s, and acceleration (2,0,0) m/s² in both frames.
